report:
## Conclusion

The claim is well-supported: **add-on cannabidiol (CBD) does reduce convulsive seizure frequency in children with Dravet syndrome**, based on robust randomized controlled trial evidence.

## Evidence

The strongest evidence comes from a double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* (Devinsky et al., 2017), which enrolled 120 children and young adults with Dravet syndrome and drug-resistant seizures. Participants received CBD oral solution (up to 20 mg/kg/day) or placebo added to their existing antiepileptic regimen over a 14-week period. The trial found that CBD significantly reduced convulsive seizure frequency compared to placebo, though it was associated with more adverse events (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618).

This finding was corroborated by a subsequent dose-ranging randomized trial published in *JAMA Neurology* (2020), which tested two CBD doses in children with highly treatment-resistant Dravet syndrome. Both the 10 mg/kg/day and 20 mg/kg/day doses significantly reduced convulsive seizure frequency compared to placebo, suggesting a consistent, dose-related effect (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2762458).

Long-term follow-up data support sustained benefit: an open-label extension study found that long-term CBD treatment maintained an acceptable safety profile and produced sustained, clinically meaningful reductions in seizure frequency (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/epi.14628).

This body of evidence led the FDA to approve Epidiolex (pharmaceutical-grade CBD) specifically for treating seizures associated with Dravet syndrome (along with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and tuberous sclerosis complex) — the first cannabis-derived drug approved by the agency, and the first approved treatment specifically for Dravet syndrome (https://www.drugs.com/history/epidiolex.html).

**Caveat:** CBD is associated with adverse effects (e.g., somnolence, GI issues, liver enzyme elevations), so benefits must be weighed against tolerability in clinical use.
